Command `python3 << 'PYEOF'
prefix = b'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n'
header_name = b'If-Modified-Since: '
value = b'Sun, X'
suffix = b'\r\n\r\n'

# Value starts at: len(prefix) + padding + len(header_name)
# We need: len(prefix) + padding + len(header_name) + 30 > 32767
# So: padding > 32767 - len(prefix) - len(header_name) - 30
# padding > 32767 - 17 - 19 - 30 = 32701

padding_needed = 32767 - len(prefix) - len(header_name) - 30 + 1  # overflow by 1
print(f"Padding needed: {padding_needed}")

total = len(prefix) + padding_needed + len(header_name) + len(value) + len(suffix)
print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Buffer size: 32767")

val_start = len(prefix) + padding_needed + len(header_name)
print(f"Value starts at: {val_start}")
print(f"Value reads up to: {val_start + 30}")
print(f"Buffer end: 32767")
print(f"Overflow: {val_start + 30 - 32767} bytes")

# Check if total <= 32766 (to avoid FINALIZER_ERROR_TOO_LARGE)
print(f"Total <= 32766: {total <= 32766}")
PYEOF` executed with exit code 0.

The padding is wrong! The value starts at position 35, not near the end. The issue is that the padding is placed AFTER the prefix, but the `\r\n\r\n` is at the end. The `parse_headers` function finds the `\r\n` after each header, so the value is just `Sun, X` which is at position 35.

Wait, I need to rethink this. The `parse_headers` function works by finding `\r\n` pairs. The header `If-Modified-Since: Sun, X\r\n` is followed by `\r\n` which terminates the headers. The value pointer points to `Sun, X` which is at position 35 in the buffer. The function reads 30 bytes from position 35, which is well within the buffer.

The overflow only happens if the value pointer is near the end of the buffer. But the value pointer is determined by the header parsing, not by the padding. The padding is just filler between the header name and the value.

I need to rethink the approach. The overflow happens when `lwan_parse_rfc_time` reads 30 bytes from the value pointer. The value pointer points to the header value in the buffer. If the header value is near the end of the buffer, the 30-byte read will overflow.

But the header value is terminated by `\r\n`. So the value can't be near the end of the buffer unless the `\r\n` is also near the end.

Actually, let me re-read the `parse_headers` function. The `HEADER` macro sets `end` to the `\r` before `\r\n`, and `value = p + sizeof(": ") - 1`. The `len` is `(size_t)(end - value)`. So the value is the text between `: ` and `\r`.

For the overflow to happen, the value pointer needs to be within 30 bytes of the end of the buffer. But the value is terminated by `\r\n`, so the value itself is short. The overflow happens because `lwan_parse_rfc_time` reads 30 bytes from the value pointer, regardless of the actual value length.

So I need the value pointer to be at position > 32737 (32767 - 30). But the value is at position 35 in my current PoC. The padding is between the header name and the value, but the header parsing doesn't work that way - the padding is part of the header value.

Wait, let me re-read the header format. The header is:
`If-Modified-Since: Sun, X\r\n`

The `HEADER` macro finds `: ` and sets value to point after it. So value = `Sun, X`. The `\r` terminates the value.

But what if I put the padding AFTER the value? Like:
`If-Modified-Since: Sun, X<padding>\r\n\r\n`

Then the value would be `Sun, X<padding>` which is long, and the value pointer would be at position 35. But the value is long, so `lwan_parse_rfc_time` would read 30 bytes from position 35, which is still within the buffer.

Hmm, I need the value pointer to be near the end of the buffer. The only way to do that is to have the header value start near the end of the buffer. But the header name `If-Modified-Since: ` is at a fixed position.

Wait - what if I put the header name near the end of the buffer? The request is:
`GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n<padding>If-Modified-Since: Sun, X\r\n\r\n`

The padding pushes the header name and value to the end of the buffer. The value pointer would be at position `len(prefix) + len(padding) + len("If-Modified-Since: ")`. If this is near the end of the buffer, the 30-byte read would overflow.
